name: Violence Against Women Directive
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: Commission forecasts and a fresh survey baseline; transposition not due until 2027
summary: The Commission forecast that the Directive could save the EU economy around EUR 53 billion a year by reducing violence against women, against EUR 5-6.6 billion in compliance costs. Countries have until 2027 to apply it, so there is no evidence yet on its effect; a 2024 EU survey, finding that about one in three women have experienced physical or sexual violence or threats, provides the starting point for future evaluation.

indicators.objective: Comparable administrative data on violence against women
indicators.indicator: Common disaggregations and methodology developed by EIGE; data collection tool and guidelines deployed; number of Member States able to report data on all forms of violence covered (availability) and in full compliance (comparability) each year
indicators.evidence: Directive adopted May 2024; transposition deadline June 2027, so no Member State reporting under the Directive yet. Baseline exists from the joint Eurostat-FRA-EIGE EU gender-based violence survey (key results Nov 2024).

indicators.indicator: Economic benefits of reduced prevalence about EUR 53.1bn, potentially EUR 82.7bn in the long term (mostly lower physical and emotional harm to victims, EUR 32.2-64.5bn)
indicators.evidence: Not evaluated. Survey baseline: about 1 in 3 women in the EU (30.7%) report physical violence, threats and/or sexual violence in their lifetime.

indicators.indicator: Total compliance costs EUR 5-6.6bn, mostly for Member States; about EUR 1.9bn for employers (manager training on sexual harassment)
Member States report to the Commission 7 years after entry into force; regular EU-wide surveys transmitted to Eurostat

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence (executive summary SWD(2022) 63), SWD(2022) 62
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence (executive summary SWD(2022) 63)
literature.outcomes: prevalence of violence; economic cost of violence; compliance costs
literature.headline: Preferred option 2A: reduced prevalence could bring economic benefits of around EUR 53.1bn, up to EUR 82.7bn in the long term; compliance costs EUR 5-6.6bn, mostly borne by Member States, EUR 1.9bn by employers; no negative impacts noted
literature.summary_plain: The Commission estimated that the law could save around EUR 53 billion (up to EUR 83 billion in the long run) by reducing violence, against EUR 5-6.6 billion in costs, mostly for national authorities.

literature.citation: Eurostat, EU Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA) & European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) (2024), EU gender-based violence survey - key results (2024 edition), Eurostat/FRA/EIGE joint publication, 25 November 2024
literature.authors: Eurostat, EU Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA) & European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE)
literature.title: EU gender-based violence survey - key results (2024 edition)
literature.method: descriptive (survey of about 114,000 women aged 18-74, fieldwork Sept 2020-Mar 2024)
literature.headline: About 1 in 3 women in the EU (30.7%) have experienced physical violence, threats and/or sexual violence; about 1 in 6 sexual violence including rape; 1 in 5 violence by a partner, relative or household member
literature.summary_plain: The EU's first joint survey since the Directive was proposed found about one in three women have experienced physical or sexual violence or threats - the baseline against which the Directive will be judged.
literature.quality: baseline only; not an impact study
